content_voiceover: This slide, from the Gunay-Aygun natural history study of Gray Platelet Syndrome in Blood 2010, shows why this disorder is progressive rather than static. The scatter plot on the top left tracks platelet count against age across the patient cohort, and the trend line declines steadily from over two hundred thousand in infancy toward the twenty to fifty thousand range by adulthood. The bone marrow reticulin stains, panels B through E, show progressively increasing fibrosis, believed to result from abnormal release of growth factors like PDGF and TGF-beta from megakaryocytes that cannot properly package them into alpha granules. The electron micrographs below confirm the ultrastructural defect directly, both platelets show a normal dense tubular system and open canalicular system, but the alpha granules are essentially absent or severely reduced, explaining the gray appearance seen on light microscopy. Exam takeaway, unlike Bernard-Soulier or MYH9 disease which have relatively stable counts, Gray Platelet Syndrome worsens over decades with progressive marrow fibrosis and splenomegaly.
keypoints: Platelet count declines progressively with age in Gray Platelet Syndrome
Bone marrow reticulin fibrosis worsens over time
EM: alpha granules (AG) absent/reduced; DTS and OCS preserved
GPS is progressive - unlike relatively static BSS/MYH9 counts
keypoint_voiceover: Gray Platelet Syndrome is progressive, platelet counts fall steadily with age and bone marrow fibrosis worsens over decades, likely from unpackaged growth factors leaking out of megakaryocytes. Electron microscopy confirms a normal dense tubular system and open canalicular system but near-absent alpha granules. Contrast this progressive course with the relatively stable thrombocytopenia seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome and MYH9-related disease.
